justification: The conviction affirmed on appeal rests on the zoning provision capping rooms 'rented for lodging or boarding purposes' in a residential district; the court expressly distinguishes this from the separate 'lodging house' licensing ordinance (under which defendants were acquitted) and holds the two are not inconsistent, meaning the employee-occupancy here was still found to be use of rooms for lodging purposes under the zoning ordinance even though it fell short of a licensable lodging-house business.
supporting_quote: Not more than two rooms may be rented for lodging or boarding purposes in any one dwelling, and to not more than a total of four persons

justification: The court holds that an occupant of an inn room is not in 'possession of real property' and therefore the innkeeper's self-help lockout does not violate the forcible-entry statute, affirming the innkeeper's unilateral right to control and reclaim rooms without resort to court process. This squarely favors the owner's/innkeeper's control over the letting arrangement as a lawful incident of ownership, notwithstanding the court's disclaiming any moral endorsement of defendants' conduct.
supporting_quote: defendants were within their strict legal right ... they acted lawfully and are not answerable in damages to plaintiff

justification: The court enjoins both the fee owner and the prime tenant from altering the letting arrangement, holding that rent-control regulations 'override the contractual relation between them' and compel continued furnishing of services despite the prime tenant's lease having validly expired. This is a clear case of a restriction on the ordinary incidents of letting (the right to terminate and withdraw furnishings) being upheld against the property interests of both landlord and lessee, which fits 'adverse' better than either 'favorable' or 'mixed' since there is no favorable/ownership-protective holding at all — the entire ruling subordinates contract and ownership rights to the regulatory scheme.
supporting_quote: the rent regulations have imposed statutory duties and a statutory relationship on the parties which override the contractual relation between them

justification: Although a 10-year lease exists between the fee owner and prime tenant, the occupants whose interests the action actually protects are the 66 'roomers' in a 'rooming house,' repeatedly described in those terms by the court; the substantive compensated-occupancy relationship at issue (individual room occupants receiving furniture/services for rent) is a lodging arrangement, not the overarching lease between owner and prime tenant.
supporting_quote: the fee owner and the prime tenant of a rooming house ... the 66 roomers are entitled to the protection of the rent laws

justification: The case does not adjudicate an occupancy relationship between an owner and an occupant at all — it enjoins construction of a proposed tourist-cabin camp under a restrictive covenant before any occupancy occurred — so none of lease/license/lodging/innkeeping fit; but the opinion does explicitly characterize the prohibited use, a compensated short-term-occupancy business, as a 'commercial enterprise,' which is best captured as 'other' rather than leaving the field blank.
supporting_quote: a tourist camp was a commercial enterprise, the operation of which was prohibited by the building restrictions governing the subdivision

justification: The plaintiff boardinghouse keeper's claim is largely defeated: three of four months' board and lodging charges are barred by the one-year prescription specific to innkeepers' claims, the washing charge fails for lack of proof, and the children's-board claim fails on the merits, with only a small $60 claim for the sick negro's board sustained. This split, largely unfavorable outcome for the party asserting the compensated-occupancy claim is better described as mixed than as a clean favorable result.
supporting_quote: The only portion of the plaintiff's claim sustained by the law and testimony, is that for the boarding and attention to the sick negro.

justification: The court imposes strict liability on the innkeeper for a lodging guest's stolen property absent forcible breaking, which is adverse to the innkeeper's interests, but it also notes the innkeeper could have avoided this liability entirely by posting a statutory notice — an available favorable route the defendant simply failed to use. justification: The opinion is explicitly framed around inn-keeper liability doctrine, citing the Civil Code articles governing innkeepers' responsibility as depositaries for guests' effects, and the underlying facts involve a traveler lodging at 'the City Hotel.' justification: The case adjudicates a lease of a dwelling let for a term with rent, including the tenant's stated purpose of running it as a boarding house, squarely implicating the legal character of a compensated letting arrangement and a landlord's duties/misrepresentations in connection with it. 'Letting' is explicitly within the corpus's scope, and this opinion turns entirely on lease formation, habitability, and rent liability.
supporting_quote: The lease in this case was for six months, from the first of November to the first of May following, the rent being payable monthly in advance.

justification: The opinion restates the general rule protecting landlords (no implied warranty of habitability, no duty to disclose known defects absent inquiry) but carves out liability where the landlord affirmatively and knowingly misrepresents the premises' condition to induce the tenant to forgo inspection. Because it both reaffirms the landlord's ordinary caveat-emptor protections and restricts enforcement of the lease in the fraud scenario, the outcome is neither purely favorable to letting-as-ownership-incident nor a straightforward restriction/regulation of letting.
supporting_quote: There is no implied warranty on the part of a landlord that a house is fit for occupation ... but a material representation by him to the tenant, which he knows to be false, as to the condition of the house, and upon which representation he is advised at the time the tenant for certain reasons means to rely upon, is quite another matter.

justification: The court repeatedly refers to the instrument and relationship as a lease with a fixed term and monthly rent, and treats the obligations (repair covenant, rent liability) under ordinary landlord-tenant lease doctrine rather than as a license, lodging, or innkeeping relationship.

justification: The court expressly concedes that, even treating the defendant as bound by a lodging-house keeper's duty of ordinary care, the case turns on the lodger's own contributory negligence rather than on any categorical protection or restriction of the letting relationship itself. justification: The decision upholds the landlord's statutory summary-dispossession remedy against a tenant of a furnished house, and separately affirms that a landlord may distrain for rent on furnished lodgings, treating rent-collection and eviction remedies as lawful incidents of the letting/ownership relationship rather than restricting them.

supporting_quote: That there was a sufficient consideration for the promise admits of no ground for doubt.

justification: The court never classifies the arrangement as a lease, license, lodging, or innkeeping relationship; the boarding is incidental background to a pure consideration/contract-liability dispute, so no characterization value applies.
